claims.text: Rapid dynamic recovery occurs during room-temperature deformation of equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi solid solution.
Dynamic recovery limits dislocation accumulation during room-temperature deformation.
Limited dislocation accumulation causes low work hardening, hardness, and strength.
Suppressing dynamic recovery increases dislocation storage.
Increased dislocation storage produces higher hardness and strength.
The applicable starting material is solution-annealed, single-phase FCC-based equimolar or near-equimolar CoCrFeNiTi with a pristine solid-solution structure.
The controlled comparison is between room-temperature and approximately 77 K tensile and nanoindentation tests at approximately 10^-4 s^-1.
Dislocation density and dislocation configurations, including cells and recovery-induced substructures, mediate the proposed temperature dependence of mechanical behavior.
Dislocations have high mobility at room temperature in this alloy.
Lower stacking-fault energy and an FCC structure with multiple slip systems contribute to high dislocation mobility.
Dynamic recovery proceeds through dislocation climb and cross-slip.
Room-temperature tests will show lower hardness, yield strength, and ultimate tensile strength than cryogenic tests.
Room-temperature TEM will show fewer, more widely spaced dislocations in a recovered configuration.
Cryogenic TEM will show a higher density of entangled dislocations.
The predicted temperature-dependent differences will occur without deformation twinning or phase transformation.
The hypothesis is limited to solution-annealed, single-phase FCC-based equimolar or near-equimolar CoCrFeNiTi deformed from the elastic-plastic transition to moderate plastic strain.
Failure to observe both increased dislocation density and increased hardness and strength at 77 K would falsify the dynamic-recovery hypothesis.
